book: 075 - Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo
samples: Robert Arp's introduction argues Psych is perfect for philosophy because Henry's games train observation and inference exactly as philosophers hone them, while Shawn's ruse shows how clever people abuse those powers to deceive - quoting Machiavelli's line that one who deceives will always find those who allow themselves to be deceived. It sets up the book's recurring ethical question about lying: lies for the liar's profit (Shawn avoiding jail in the pilot), paternalistic lies for the hearer's own good (Henry telling seven-year-old Shawn he 'blacked out' about his mother's death), and lies to benefit many (promising a terrorist freedom to find his bomb). Since Shawn's lies solve cases and save lives, the introduction suggests they may not be so bad in the end, though it admits wishing he would just come clean as a talented honest detective.

Michaud argues that Shawn's whole psychic career runs on fallacies of relevance - the red herring of claiming to be psychic to dodge arrest, plus ad hominem mockery that deflects Lassiter's fraud accusations - so the show's comedy turns on bad logic being used to lead people to true conclusions. Socrates supplies the opposing voice: like the Sophists who argued any side for money, Shawn reasons for convenience and amusement, and his deception is an inconsistency of the kind Socrates refused in Plato's Crito, where he would not bribe his way out of a death sentence. An invented Platonic-style dialogue has Socrates question Shawn until he concedes that lying breeds more lying and harm - 'her name is Truth!' - before Shawn escapes the elenchus by spotting lipstick on Socrates's collar. The chapter leaves the verdict open: Shawn saves lives and raises the world's happiness, but his trickery also trains Santa Barbara to reason badly and trust con artists.

Muniz plays narratologist, arguing that what matters in Psych is not the story but the storyteller: the 1980s prologues, alias gags, pineapples, and Lassie feuds are recurring formula elements, while Shawn's eidetic-memory sequence - the raised eyebrow, the chime, the highlighted detail - is the one necessary element around which every episode's rising action, climax, and denouement are arranged. Asking whether Gus chatting at the aquarium dolphins or the characters' comic pauses break the fourth wall, he answers no: the eidetic sequences only produce a 'projective illusion of cinematic image' that makes viewers feel they see through Shawn's eyes, so the wall is never actually broken - the show simply 'psychs you out in the end.' The chapter even structures itself like a Psych episode, prologue to climax, to prove the point that structure is function.

Jones argues that Shawn's 'psychic' act is really hypersensory perception (HSP) - noticing cat fur, fine print, blood spatter - feeding inference to the best explanation (IBE), the natural abductive method Sherlock Holmes mislabels deduction, with Clever Hans and Ilga Kirks as real-world parallels. Applying IBE with Ockham's Razor to the two hypotheses 'he's psychic' versus 'he's hyper-observant,' she concludes the natural explanation should win for everyone: Lassiter's skepticism tracks the evidence, Gus knows better despite believing in ghosts, and Chief Vick shouldn't buy the supernatural story either. Juliet's belief survives only through background supernatural beliefs, a psychic-friendly culture, and ignoring the clues Gus feeds Shawn, which the chapter diagnoses as the same public misunderstanding of the scope and limits of science that keeps most Americans believing in ESP.

Yim argues that what onlookers mistake for psychic power is thin-slicing, Gladwell's rapid pattern-recognition, the same skill behind John Gottman's ninety-percent-accurate marriage predictions and Paul Ekman's involuntary micro-expressions, which is how Shawn acquits the telenovela actor in 'Lights, Camera,... Homicidio' by reading genuine surprise on the tape. Criminals deceive by staging a context - a gun by the suicide's hand - that biases investigators the way thinking 'forest' biases us toward 'black bear,' while Shawn's two-stage slice, gut instinct plus conscious interpretation, isolates the telltale detail (a marinated steak in the fridge) that the staging was designed to bury. Henry's flashbacks - the cereal box opened from the bottom, young Shawn reading poker tells in the locker room - are boot camp that trains him to think outside conventional frames, producing the 'tint on the windows to the soul' certitude he invokes in 'Cloudy... with a Chance of Murder.'

The Senors use Psych to separate true belief from knowledge: Shawn's hunch that Shabby the sea lion was murdered is true but shabbily evidenced, and his justified, true belief that a Clayton family member sabotaged the plane fails to be knowledge when the killer turns out to be a son-in-law he had no reason to think existed - a textbook Gettier case from 'He Dead.' They then weigh the two main theories of justification, evidentialism (with its base rates and prior probabilities) and reliabilism, and both vindicate the careful, methodical work of Lassiter and Juliet while Shawn's trigger-happy belief-forming habit strikes out twice. Shawn is redeemed only as an evidence-generator whose disregard for priors takes 'impossible' suspects like a murdered sea lion seriously, so that pairing his talents with the detectives' rigor yields the complete detective.

book: 076 - The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia
samples: The editors introduce the book by contrasting The Good Wife with earlier law shows like Law and Order: for the first time we see lawyers at home, and the central figure is Alicia Florrick, juggling teenagers, a firm in bankruptcy, and a marriage wrecked by Peter's prostitution scandal while keeping up appearances as the 'good wife' and taking lover Will Gardner. They argue the show refuses a single right answer - her choices are selfish, cowardly, vengeful, or simply her being true to herself - and that her growth as a woman, mother, and lawyer challenges preconceived social norms about women and about lawyers. Philosophy enters as the natural sequel: ethics, justice, feminism, privacy rights, epistemology, and social-political philosophy are all sewn into the episodes.

Judith Andre uses the show's cases - Alicia's overnight prison visit to Peter for case information in 'Conjugal', snatching evidence before the police in 'Hi', Kalinda's inadmissible but coercive evidence in 'Heart', and Will's advice to use perjured testimony in 'Long Way Home' - to ask whether the profession's zealous advocacy actually serves justice. She explains the adversary system's two-level defense (each side's pursuit of victory supposedly forces truth out, mirroring sport) and its weaknesses: money decides outcomes, and no one in the courtroom is responsible for the truth, as the buried Childs tapes in 'Hybristophilia' show. Individual liberty against state power justifies criminal defense at most, and she endorses David Luban's sober conclusion that the system is justified yet 'cannot mandate lawyers to cut throats', with Alicia remaining the show's uneasy, unreconciled conscience.

Jai Galliott takes the Season Three episode 'Whiskey Tango Foxtrot', in which Nevada-based drone operator Sergeant Elkins kills twelve Afghan civilians and is convicted of murder despite Alicia's scapegoating defense, as a case study in the ethics of drone warfare. Tracing just war theory from the Mahabharata through Augustine to Aquinas's jus ad bellum and jus in bello framework, he applies proportionality and discrimination to the strike and argues that sensor limits and the physical and emotional distance of push-button killing (Grossman's spectrum from knife combat to drones) erode operators' capacity for discriminate targeting. He concludes that drones are a moral hazard but a legitimate asset, and that blame must be apportioned among operator, manufacturer, and commanders rather than dumped on Elkins alone.

Rod Carveth maps Bentham's act-utilitarianism onto Lockhart Gardner's defense-side reasoning and Mill's rule-utilitarianism onto the prosecution's, then tests the pairing on the firm's recurring client Colin Sweeney. Sweeney's cases - the wrongful-death suit in 'Bad' where Alicia says 'Of course' he killed his wife, the manslaughter plea and merger opportunism in 'Hybristophilia', and the perjured testimony Alicia may still use in 'Long Way Home' - show the firm letting the end of client and firm gain justify the means. Sweeney walking free, restored to his company, and a father despite admitting the murder is the counter-intuitive consequence that makes Carveth question whether act-utilitarianism should ground our decisions at all.

Celine Morin reads Alicia's love life through the Greek triad agape, eros, and philia as laid out in Plato's Symposium: her unconditional agape for Peter is eroded by his demands for forgiveness ('Stripped', 'Boom'), while the Socratic myth of Eros born from Penia's lack explains why she tells Will their affair is 'romantic because it didn't happen'. She argues Alicia abandons the romantic soul-mate model of her pearl-necklace marriage for Giddens's egalitarian 'pure relationship' with Will, but stays moored to the old family structure, hesitating on the doorstep in the Season Three cliffhanger 'The Dream Time'. Her discovery of feminism through Diane Lockhart is what lets Alicia weigh leaving that structure without destroying her family.

Kathleen Poorman Dougherty sets Kant's universal, emotion-free morality (echoed in Kohlberg's justice stages and Judge Abernathy's 'blind court' claim in 'Infamy') against Carol Gilligan's care ethic, which she says fits Saint Alicia far better: Alicia's practical advice to Jennifer Lewis in the pilot, driving Kenny home in 'Home', and telling Kenny's father 'I care a lot more about your son than he does' show connection producing both better morality and better lawyering. Feminist theorists like Nel Noddings and Sara Ruddick treat this care orientation as morally superior, not merely different, but the chapter's later sections weigh the cost: Kalinda's burnout warning, Alicia's resentment at always hand-holding clients, and the double bind by which women absorb society's unpaid caring labor. The verdict is that care is genuinely moral, but it must become a shared burden.

book: 077 - Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book
samples: The editors' introduction argues that Boardwalk Empire's Prohibition setting - bootleggers, corrupt politicians, G-men, and ordinary citizens at one table against the Volstead Act - puts its characters in philosophically loaded situations that bear directly on real life. It then maps the volume: Littmann reads Nucky as a Machiavellian Prince, Greene casts him as Nietzsche's Superman, Archibald reads Gillian through Plato, Brace and Kingsbury test Aristotle's happiness against Nucky, Chalky, and Margaret, and Robison-Greene treats Jimmy and Richard as war veterans facing existential problems. It closes by previewing chapters on Van Alden's God, the ethics of lying (Fallis), storytelling (Carveth) and deception (Cobb), the body politic (Schwanebeck) and the social contract (Fitzpatrick), causing versus allowing harm (Da Silva), violence (Mellamphy), and a Freudian reading of Jimmy and Gillian (Hirschbein).

Littmann tests The Prince against the real bosses behind the show - Nucky Johnson, Capone, Luciano, Rothstein, Torrio - and argues that Prohibition-era history bears out Machiavelli's rules of power. Seizing new opportunities pays (Nucky turning Atlantic City into the World's Playground, Colosimo gunned down for refusing bootlegging, Luciano eliminating Masseria and Maranzano to modernize the Mafia), and harming a rival without crushing him invites revenge (Nucky's fatal leniency toward Jimmy, Maranzano leaving the scarred Luciano alive). A ruler needs good arms, must tailor appearances to each audience (Capone's banquet murder of Anselmi and Scalise, Nucky's respectability and staged generosity), and above all must avoid hatred - the downfall of Nucky, Capone, and Luciano, and of the needlessly arrogant Rothstein, shot over a gambling debt he could easily have paid.

Greene asks whether Nucky is Nietzsche's Ubermensch and works through each criterion. Nucky, Gyp Rosetti, and the other mobsters are passionate, active shapers of their world (Van Alden fails here), and Nucky is a genuine creator of values after the death of God - his whopper to the Temperance League, his flip-flopping sermons to black and white congregations, and his 'I. Am. Not. Seeking. Forgiveness.' over Jimmy's body reject slave morality where the other gangsters merely follow the objective moral code of omerta. He sacrifices lesser lives (Hans Schroeder, Gillian) and has the required dark side, but he fails the final test of teaching the eternal recurrence, so he remains only 'well on his way' to Superman - a status the show's women (Margaret, Lucy, Gillian) never approach, hovering closer to the last man.

Hirschbein has Freud analyze the audience first: like Van Alden, the repressed hypocrite whose true self erupts in drowning Sebso and burning his workplace tormentor, we watch Nucky and Jimmy as avatars of our own repressed aggression and lust. Freud's contest of Eros and Thanatos - his reframing of Plato's tripartite soul as id, ego, and superego - explains why civilization demands renunciation while spectacle like Boardwalk supplies vicarious gratification, with Milgram's and Zimbardo's experiments showing how thin the civilized veneer is. Jimmy's seduction by his mother and killing of the Commodore enact the Oedipus complex writ large, Freud's primal-horde story of the sons' parridical revolt against the father, and the show's catharsis is what lets us live with the sin.

Brace and Kingsbury use the Nicomachean Ethics to argue that Nucky, Chalky, and Margaret mistake pleasure and the mere instruments of happiness - tailored suits, money, useful connections, the appearance of virtue - for Aristotle's stable, self-sustaining virtuous activity, so their lives stay unstable and empty. Nucky 'buys' even Jimmy and Margaret, Chalky's jail-cell staging with David Copperfield shows how fragile his facade of cultivation is, and Margaret's acquisitions end in blackmail and in bribing God over Emily's polio. Only Richard Harrow, the Tin Man whose collage-clippings represent a happiness he believes he can never have, moves toward real Aristotelian friendship through Jimmy's 'Of course I would; right down to the last bullet' - the philia Aristotle calls most necessary for a happy life.

Carveth argues that the show's historical license is ethically troubling because docudrama viewers - especially those who know nothing of 1920s Atlantic City - absorb 'reel history' as fact. He documents the blend of real and invented: Buscemi's slight Nucky Thompson against the imposing real Nucky Johnson, a fictional military past for Capone, Torrio stripped of his mentor role, and the McGarrigle episodes' misrepresentation of de Valera, Collins, and the Anglo-Irish Treaty. The deepest distortion is violence - the real Nucky ruled through jobs, ostracism, and economic coercion rather than murder, but that would not make good television - and given research showing viewers 'learn' from docudramas they know least about, Terence Winter's ninety-percent-accuracy claim amounts to an unethical misleading of the audience.

book: 078 - Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom
samples: The editors' introduction argues that Futurama is more than a cartoon: Matt Groening and David X. Cohen built a gold-standard sci-fi show whose storylines engage ethics, time travel, science, normalcy, and the environment. It frames Fry as a twenty-first-century flawed hero in the lineage of Moses, Gilgamesh, Odysseus, Don Quixote, and Frodo, called beyond his inadequacies, and reads his opening 'Space Pilot 3000' musings about the gorilla-throwing-barrels game as a glimpse of life's ups and downs. The chapter presents the show's strategy of making the mundane strange as the backdrop the volume's philosophers will use to examine life and meaning, and jokes that fans' resurrection of the canceled show (wave after wave, like Zapp Brannigan's troops) guarantees Futurama's permanence.

In 'A Taste of Freedom,' Zoidberg eats Earth's flag Old Freebie on Freedom Day, is tried by Earth's Supreme Court, and his death sentence triggers a Decapodian invasion that enslaves Earth under the Mobile Oppression Palace. The chapter pits Mill's On Liberty defense of unpopular expression (mankind cannot silence a lone dissenter; unchallenged beliefs are mere 'true opinions' akin to prejudice) against Feinberg's offense principle, mapping the case onto Texas v. Johnson and the symbolic-speech line from Stromberg to Tinker. It ends with Zoidberg burning the flag 'to preserve the freedom it represents': liberty and majority will often conflict (doomsday devices, Proposition Infinity's robosexual marriage ban), so preserving freedom requires tolerating offensive expression.

Young tests Isaiah Berlin's distinction between negative liberty (absence of external interference) and positive liberty (rational self-government) on three episodes: Fry's super-Slurm compulsion in 'Fry and the Slurm Factory,' human Bender's lethal gluttony in 'Anthology of Interest II,' and the worms whose upgrades win Leela's love in 'Parasites Lost' - each agent is externally unobstructed yet not self-governing. Bender's jacking-on addiction and the Temple of Robotology's threat of Robot Hell in 'Hell Is Other Robots' illustrate Rousseau's 'forced to be free,' the coercion that Berlin warned has licensed totalitarian regimes. The chapter concludes Futurama takes no side, suggesting genuine freedom needs both positive and negative liberty.

Buchanan reads 'A Big Piece of Garbage' as political ecology: the trash ball Old New York blasted into space in 2000 returns to threaten New New York, showing that even a society that has 'mastered recycling' cannot escape a capitalist economy whose commodities are designed to end as waste. On the trash ball, Fry's nostalgia ('junk isn't garbage... a glorious monument to the twentieth century') debates Leela's 'this stuff was garbage when it was new,' and Fry's rescue plan - building a second trash ball to knock the first into the Sun - merely recreates the disaster, celebrated as 'the twentieth-century spirit' of willful ignorance. Drawing on Bryant and Bailey's political ecology and Rodgers's waste stream, the chapter argues trash unmasks the exploitation of nature crystallized in commodities, so green technology and recycling alone cannot avert ecological crisis.

Malloy defines war as organized, political, violent conflict and tests Futurama's many invasions against just war theory: Zapp's invasion of Spheron 1 in 'War Is the H-Word' fails just cause ('they stand for everything we don't stand for'), the first Omicronian invasion over the interrupted Single Female Lawyer broadcast fails proportionality and last resort, while the second, over eaten Popplers, passes. Zapp's Hyperdeath laser ribbon-cutting and the Bender suicide-bombing plot against the Brain Balls illustrate discrimination, proportionality, and means evil in themselves, and the postwar demand that Lrrr eat one human - ending with blameless Free Waterfall Jr. - raises war-crimes punishment and restitution. The chapter closes by endorsing Walzer: a state's moral authority hinges on at least acknowledging the rules of war.

Piven argues Zapp Brannigan's 'sexlexia' - his deluded velour-and-spanking seductions of Leela and his relief at finding Lee Lemon is a woman - typifies a whole cast of clueless lovers (Fry coaching Zoidberg's courtship of Edna, Morgan Proctor's mess fetish, Bender coldly dumping the Planet Express ship in 'Love and Rocket'). Kant's condemnation of masturbation as self-abuse that throws away one's personality and violates humanity in one's own person is exposed as unsupported prejudice, and Nietzsche's claim that morality projects fear, envy, and disgust onto the despised other explains why 'perversion' is an arbitrary cultural judgment. Freud, Stoller, and McDougall then recast perversion as unconscious flight from anxiety and death, so the show's kink - up to the Monsterpus of The Beast with a Billion Backs and Amy's 'general sluttiness' - mirrors our own sexlexia and existential dread.

book: 079 - Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth
samples: The editor's introduction surveys the sprawling Frankenstein pop-culture corpus the book will dissect - Whale's 1931 'It's Alive!' scene, the lovable Herman Munster, Mel Brooks's Young Frankenstein, Dean Koontz's Dr. Helios, Boris Karloff's grunting brute, and I, Frankenstein's Adam - insisting the creature now lives in hundreds of films, shows, and novels rather than Shelley's text alone. It frames the book's guiding shocks: whether a re-animated corpse-man has a soul, whether making monsters differs from making babies, and whether Frankenstein's maligned creation would be right to seek to end all of us. It closes by inviting readers to peer into the monster's dull yellow eyes with the lights left on and the door barred.

Hauskeller argues Shelley's Victor was sane and benevolently motivated, and reads the 'playing God' warning (Whale's 'now I know what it feels to be God!', the Genesis tree of life, the sorcerer's apprentice) as a claim that crossing nature's lines is dangerous rather than sinful. He then flips the story: like the creature, we are children abandoned by a creator who withholds eternal life, so the real wrong is a creator's failure of duty and love - while Epicurus's death-is-nothing-to-us argument and the picture of a childless, static immortal world undermine the transhumanist case that death is the greatest evil. The chapter ends with Aristotle's mean: obsessive pursuit of knowledge and immortality wrecks happiness, which lies in discovering that our native town is the world and living in the present.

Chaib reads Craig Venter's 2010 synthetic bacterium 'Synthia' as a real-world Victor Frankenstein and tests it against Habermas's The Future of Human Nature, which condemns liberal eugenics because turning reproduction into manufacture undermines moral equality, rights, and autonomy - the same irresponsible isolation that made Victor abandon his creature and doom Justine. Rousseau and Thomas More supply the counter-program: hunger persists through unequal property ('This is mine'), not scarcity, so improving the human heart and social structures beats Venter's engineered fixes. Frankenweenie - where pets reanimated without love turn evil while Victor's beloved Sparky saves the town - lands the chapter's Arendtian moral that 'to live' is always plural (inter homines esse), so creators must care about their creations' relations with others.

Littmann argues that stripped of religious scruple, Shelley's own supreme virtue - kindness, embodied in Victor's family, Elizabeth, Clerval, and the cottagers - actually supports creating artificial life: the monster is benevolent until mistreated, and superior corpse-people would be a race of geniuses rather than a threat we may preemptively suppress. The monster himself invents utilitarianism ('relative as they were, as I applied them, to pleasure and pain alone'), De Lacey nearly lives it by promising the stranger rehabilitation over punishment, but Victor's case against building a mate is exposed as speciesism - he tallies unborn humans' futures while ignoring the joys of unborn cadaver folk, though utilitarians were the first to speak for animal rights. Since intelligent otherness is humanity's only chance at non-human friendship and the risks of Prometheus's fire paid off, the chapter rewrites the modern Prometheus as a blessing and ends with a re-imagined creation scene where the monster says 'I love you' to a Victor who finally names him Nigel.

Jacquette treats Frankenstein as the modern myth of scientific overreach whose two-century grip on pop culture (over a thousand films, Frankenberry cereal) rests on three stitched-together ingredients: Enlightenment faith in applied science, the mortality-awareness of the logician's 'All men are mortal,' and Prometheus-style retribution for challenging nature - while insisting Shelley's tale is science fiction, not supernatural. Victor's real crime is not daring science but abandoning his nameless creation to raise itself, so that 'if he had taken appropriate care of the monster he made, he might not have made such a monster.' The chapter closes with Wittgenstein's remark (Philosophical Investigations §261) that philosophy ends in the wish to 'emit an inarticulate sound,' matched to the Creature's ultimate question 'What was I?' answered only with groans, as Igor's hunting horn fades over the credits of Young Frankenstein.

Casetta and Tambolo dissect the 'Frankenfood' metaphor: metaphors map a familiar source domain (the Monster) onto a poorly known target (genetically modified organisms, like the 'Frankenfish' salmon), but the mapping fails because the Monster is a genetically heterogeneous chimera assembled from dead bodies while the engineered salmon is a genetically homogeneous hybrid grown from a single fertilized egg. Framing the question with Aristotle's view of metaphysics as the study of what things ultimately are, and applying Kripke-style origin essentialism and natural-kind essentialism, they show that being a patchwork is no essential property at all - our own symbiotic bacteria outnumber our 'human' cells - so Monster and GMO are not entities of the same kind. The metaphor should be discarded as intellectual junk, yet its allure persists because the living corpse-patchwork disturbs our fantasy of ourselves as pure, unmixed organisms.

book: 080 - Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play
samples: Kevin Decker's introduction traces Card's debt to Asimov's Foundation and its 'psychohistory,' and notes the novel's surprising resonance with military readers such as the army helicopter pilot who drew courage from Ender during flight school. It previews the volume's five parts as an escalating set of questions: whether Battle School's engineered childhood can be justified, how empathy and game-playing make a commander, whether the buggers are enemies or misunderstood others, who bears responsibility for xenocide, and how Peter and Valentine's anonymous net politics remakes Earth.

Cam Cobb weighs Battle School against competing philosophies of education: Plato's Republic supplies vocational sorting by natural aptitude (complete with the myth of the metals as a 'noble lie'), while Socratic dialogue and Paulo Freire's problem-posing pedagogy demand the shared critical inquiry Ender never gets. He argues Graff's curriculum is almost purely vocational - military history, tactics, the Giant's Drink, battleroom drills - leaving no liberal paideia, and that the teachers' constant rule-changing leaves Ender feeling like 'someone's pawn,' exactly the banking-style teacher domination Freire warned against.

Jeremy Proulx reads Ender through F.W.J. Schelling's account of evil as a real, positive force rather than Augustine's mere privation of good: Ender's kicks to Stilson and Bonzo, his killing of the Giant in the mind game, and his 'I destroy them' confession all display the 'contraction into the self' Schelling thinks haunts every moral agent. He argues Graff deliberately isolates Ender to force this dark ground to the surface, and that Valentine's 'welcome to the human race' and the hive-queen's forgiveness teach Ender that evil, though never excusable, can be understood and atoned for - his fate also shows freedom tainted by a necessity we neither choose nor control.

Jeff Ewing argues the moral fabric of Ender's Game is virtue-ethical, first testing Ender's leadership against Plato's cardinal virtues, tripartite soul, and rigid class hierarchy of the Republic, then finding Aristotle a far better fit. Ender's trademark use of the minimum force necessary against Stilson, Bonzo, and the buggers sits at Aristotle's mean between cowardice and excess, while his adaptability and disregard for rules and hierarchy only count as virtues in Aristotle's framework - though his ignorance of crucial facts explains why xenocide, like his beatings, fell outside the mean.

Chad Timm applies Foucault's disciplinary power to the International Fleet: Graff sorts monitored children like 'formless clay,' watches them through a Battle School Panopticon of head monitors and battleroom observation, and uses constant testing and the normalizing gaze to make Ender his own overseer and construct the identity of a commander. He closes by mapping the same sort-examine-discipline circuit onto standardized testing and Race to the Top, noting Ender's flicker of resistance when the children finally see through the adults' game.

Andrew Zimmerman Jones argues Ender's genius is empathy cashed out through game theory: from Plato's Laches on courage to Hume's account of sympathy, sizing up the enemy's thinking is the winning strategy, and Ender's love ('in that very moment I also love him') reframes conflicts with Peter and the buggers so they can end rather than merely be won. His one failure is never extending this empathy to Graff and Rackham, so he cannot see that his final battleroom rule-breaking - 'the enemy's gate is down' - is exactly the move the adults' larger game was designed to produce.

samples: The chapter poses the 'Barney Paradox': viewers identify and empathize with a character who is utterly awful (selling a woman, the Scuba Diver con that dupes all his friends), even though we would shun him in real life. Nanay tests and finds insufficient several explanations - Barney is just immature, we only feel schadenfreude at his slap-bet punishments, or his emotions are simply contagious - since none explains why Barney's badness increases our engagement. Using Hitchcock's bomb-under-the-table example and Adam Smith's idea of imagining ourselves in another's situation, he argues identification targets the character's situation, which is not itself evil. The appeal is vicarious badness: fiction lets us be 'virtual tourists' in immorality we would never choose for real.

The chapter takes Barney's 'when I get sad, I stop being sad and be awesome instead' as a serious thesis about emotional control. Goffin surveys somatic theories (William James: control the body, fake it till you make it), cognitivist judgment theories (Sartre and Robert Solomon: Ted's rage at Barney for sleeping with Robin is a judgment of betrayal), and Jesse Prinz's 'embodied appraisal' synthesis, concluding emotions are two-stage processes of direct appraisal plus narrative monitoring. Because we partly author the narratives wrapping our appraisals - as Barney did when reinventing himself after Shannon dumped him, and as Lily does by owning her failure as a painter - we can responsibly 'awesomize' our emotions.

The chapter argues Barney is best understood as a committed ethical egoist, distinguishing egoism from egotism, immoralism, and moral skepticism through the Playbook's Scuba Diver scam. Ainsworth rejects psychological egoism (Joey's view in Friends) using evolution and apparent counterexamples like Marshall's Christmas Eve deliveries, then uses Glaucon's ring of Gyges from the Republic to ask whether anyone would resist injustice with guaranteed impunity. The friendship objection is dissolved via Aristotle's 'a friend is another self': once friends are included in the ego, saving Marshall's relationship or rushing to Ted's hospital bed counts as self-interest, constrained like chess by absolute rules such as the Bro Code's Article 150.

The chapter reads Robin's series-long arc as an argument for non-essentialist feminism against Carol Gilligan's suggestion that all women share fundamental traits and rules. Caught between Lily's Dreamhouse-Barbie domesticity and the Career-Barbie ideal her father forcibly raised her into - mocked by kindergartners at career day, 'called slut' by Marshall for a one-night stand in 'The Naked Man' - Robin keeps trying to live one prescribed path entirely and is miserable both times. Only when she stops choosing between the boxes, marrying Barney while still never wanting children, does the show endorse the non-essentialist feminism of Deborah Rhode and Drucilla Cornell: a woman may custom-tailor her own happy ending.

The chapter uses Sartre to diagnose Barney's fixed persona of suits, womanizing, and Bro Code worship as bad faith: having freely chosen to become the suited businessman who stole Shannon, Barney now acts as if those are his only options, denying his radical freedom. Hardy maps Sartre's own examples onto the show - Wendy the Waitress play-acting a stereotypical waitress, the woman who ignores the knee-touch, Barney tuning out criticism with 'I'm awesome' - and reads emotions, via Sartre's Sketch for a Theory of the Emotions, as magical transformations of the world like Marshall's 'best burger' quest and the Bob Barker paternity story. Barney's love for Robin and his secret reunion of Marshall and Lily are the moments he breaks out of bad faith and chooses freely against his persona.

The chapter argues the Bro Code's real value lies not in getting laid but in structuring homosocial bonds, listing its best articles (loyalty, equality, generosity) alongside its most sexist ones (the Hot/Crazy Scale, Article 101). Karioris explains men's competitive relations through hegemonic masculinity - the school-bully dominance that forces all masculinities to compete and pushes women out - and invokes Foucault's 'Friendship as a Way of Life' for how bonds between men can escape taboo and emotional distance. Robin as wingwoman ('a better Ted than Ted') and the gang's gender transgressions show the Code can be amended toward equality, with Aristotle's friendship of mutual cooperation and benefit, 'quid pro bro', as the standard.

book: 082 - Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying
samples: The editors' introduction argues that Crichton was doing philosophy rather than science: he imagined a possibility and probed its range because it could not be tested. It frames the whole book around Malcolm's question of whether we should, not whether we can, and around the gap between what we can do and what we should do with technologies like de-extinction. It connects the film to our illusion of control, insisting there are no ghosts or magic here, only nature, and that forgetting how edible we are turns us into 'bloody smears on the teeth of a T. rex'.

Michaud and Watkins blame Crichton and Malcolm for frightening us away from science, arguing that most life does not 'find a way' and that science is the shield keeping vulnerable humanity a step ahead of extinction by meteors, plagues, and predators. They take up Rousseau's anti-Enlightenment longing to return to nature and reject it, arguing that humility comes from science itself (a 13.72-billion-year-old Earth, Sagan's 'star stuff' making us the universe become conscious of itself), not from abandoning it. Hammond, not science, embodies the real arrogance: he was so certain he could not fail that he tested the park on his own grandchildren.

Littmann surveys real de-extinction efforts (George Church's passenger pigeon, plans to clone a frozen mammoth) and asks when reviving extinct species is morally permissible. He argues that Arne Naess's deep ecology, with its 'equal right to live and blossom', fails because it projects human desires onto organisms like plants that have none, and cannot say whether species or only individuals bear rights. He instead applies Mill's utilitarianism: bring species back when doing so maximizes happiness and minimizes suffering, which permits a Jurassic Park in principle but forbids dinosaur fights and trophy hunts like Roland Tembo's, and rebukes Sattler's claim that only the people we love matter.

Freeman explains why Grant dismisses the clones as 'genetically engineered theme park monsters': a frog-DNA-patched genome is not dinosaur DNA, and nobody knows how much alteration turns a T. rex into something else, so as Wu tells Hammond the park has only reconstructed the past, never re-created it. Behavior cannot vindicate the clones either, since The Lost World's raptors grow up without elders to teach raptor behavior, and the animals must survive an ecosystem of grass, bacteria, and species that did not exist in the Cretaceous. The chapter's running puzzle of how much of an organism can change before it is no longer that organism is a Ship of Theseus problem applied to paleontology.

Shea stages the Wu-Malcolm dispute through Hume's Dialogues: Jurassic Park is an 'intelligent design' so botched that, like Philo's world of needless suffering, it points to ignorant or malicious designers rather than a perfect God, undercutting Richard Owen-style design arguments. He then explains Hammond's folly with Darwinian natural selection and memetics, treating the dinosaur-theme-park as a meme that infected InGen's investors by exploiting evolved desires for profit, fame, and importance. Hammond's fatal errors were assuming evolution 'wants' humans to survive, that complexity means better adapted, and that he could outsmart selection, which the all-female raptors breeding and life 'finding a way' quickly refute.

A pub dialogue applies Aristotle's De Anima, where the soul is the first principle of living things, to cloning: since a living clone must have an emergent, unrepeatable soul, successfully cloning dinosaurs brings new life into existence, which is good, so cloning itself is ethical. It then argues that neither unguided natural selection nor a divine dragon-slayer who nonetheless allowed cloning technology gives us reason not to revive dinosaurs, against Malcolm's 'they had their shot'. But drawing on Plato's forms, it condemns Hammond for controlling rather than merely containing: the lysine contingency and enforced sterility leave the dinosaurs shadows of what they could be, denied their natural flourishing.

book: 083 - The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game
samples: Robert Arp's introduction opens with Halloween culture and his own seminarian past to ask whether belief in the Devil can survive scrutiny. He lays out a 'just deserts' argument - Hitler, Stalin, and Mao died unpunished while Job, Socrates, and Thomas More died unrewarded, so God, the Devil, Heaven, and Hell must exist to balance the scales - and then answers it with Freud's projection critique (religion as wishful thinking for comfort and moral control) and with the neuroscience tying the mind to a dying brain, which undermines the soul that Hell would punish. The chapter frames the whole book's project: testing devil-belief with arguments and evidence rather than taking it on authority.

Nicolas Michaud catalogues the demonic hierarchy - de Spina's goblins, incubi, and familiars, Dante's Malebranche, Binsfeld's seven princes of Hell - through Dungeon Keeper's Dark Mistress, World of Warcraft succubi, Se7en, Hellraiser's Pinhead, Hellboy, and Spawn. His real argument is ontological: names are power, and what we call the Devil fixes how we treat him. Recovering the Hebrew sense of 'satan' as an appointed adversary and 'Lucifer' as light-bringer (compared to Prometheus), he argues the same being could be reframed from tempter to giver of knowledge, much as naming Columbus's invasion a 'discovery' launders atrocity.

Sharon Kaye stages a fourteenth-century debate over a contradiction: Jesus truthfully prophesied that the Antichrist will come, yet the Antichrist remains free not to. Peter Aureoli denies bivalence for statements about the future, Thomas Bradwardine has God swap among infinite possible-world 'movies,' and Ockham's follower John of Mirecourt concludes that Jesus simply lied - each solution self-defeating or heretical. Using Ockham's Razor and her comic fantasy of seducing the Antichrist, Kaye argues the unsolvable prophecy problem helped discredit prophetic religion, ushered in theological determinism via Luther and Calvin, and opened a secular age.

James McLachlan splits the Satans of history into 'the Rebel' of Romanticism (Blake, Shelley's turn to Prometheus, the sexy vampires of film) and 'the Asshole' who wants to be God. Using Sartre's 'hell is other people' and the desire to be a complete being, he reads Dracula, Scarface's Tony Montana, and Bond villains as figures who cannot endure the otherness of real persons. With Bohme and especially Schelling's two wills - self-assertion and love of others - he argues evil is a positive, perverted order of pure egoism, and that not even Satan can achieve the total asshole-ness he wants, because selfhood exists only in relation to others.

Elizabeth Butterfield reads The Devil's Advocate through Sartre: Kevin Lomax's 'You set me up!' excuse - after defending the guilty Gettys and Cullen and abandoning MaryAnn - is textbook bad faith, a lie to himself about his own free choices. Milton the Devil plays existentialist, insisting 'I'm no puppeteer... I only set the stage. You pull your own strings,' until Kevin admits his vanity, his drive to win, motivated every choice. Radical freedom entails radical responsibility, and Kevin's final suicide is his last free act, chosen to keep coming out on top, while free will remains the one limit the Devil cannot breach.

Jim Berti opens with a dream-fable in which the Devil tempts him with a bank-robbing 'quick fix' for his house-buying cash crunch, then reads the Rolling Stones' 'Sympathy for the Devil' as the Devil's resume of history's atrocities - Anastasia, the Blitzkrieg, the Kennedys - where he supplies the lighter fluid but never strikes the match. The chapter argues we give God too much credit and the Devil too much blame while omitting ourselves: the Devil is the 'drug dealer of sin,' peddling the seven deadly sins as shortcuts like Rocky IV's steroids, and only effortful virtue refuses them. As the song says, 'it was you and me.'

book: 084 - Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions
samples: Jason Holt's introduction argues there is a genuine paradox in Leonard Cohen: his songs count both as high-art poetry and as popular folk/pop music, challenging the assumed absolute divide between high and popular art. Holt considers whether film auteur theory - the way Hitchcock elevates genre thriller - resolves the paradox by making Cohen a transcendent auteur, or whether the songs remain gloriously popular without any supra-popular transubstantiation. He rejects mentor Louis Dudek's charge that taking up the guitar betrayed Cohen's poetry, insisting the literary lyrics and pleasing melody are perfect complements.

Brendan Shea reads Cohen through the three Hellenistic schools. Socrates's trial in the Apology mirrors the persecuted singer of 'A Singer Must Die,' with 'Everybody Knows' and 'Democracy' voicing a Socratic mix of empathy and pessimism about whether democracy can deal rationally with its critics. Stoics such as Epictetus ground the present-focused, resigned acceptance of loss in 'Hey, That's No Way to Say Goodbye' and 'If It Be Your Will'; the Pyrrhonian skepticism of Sextus Empiricus illuminates the narrator's calming, unresolvable ignorance in 'Famous Blue Raincoat'; and the Epicurean atomism of Epicurus and Lucretius - death is nothing to us, empty desires are unsatisfiable - underlies 'A Thousand Kisses Deep.' Hypatia's murder and Cohen's 'Joan of Arc' close the chapter: the examined life is an all-consuming, sometimes fatal commitment that is nonetheless worthwhile.

Agust Magnusson argues that Cohen's 'crack in everything' credo from 'Anthem' is an existentialist celebration of brokenness against a culture demanding an unattainable perfect offering. He reads 'Waiting for the Miracle' alongside Camus's Sisyphus - the narrator stops waiting for a transcendent Answer and accepts the absurd, while 'The Future' and 'Democracy' dramatize both the fright of relativism and its resolution in humanistic hope. Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling then explains 'Hallelujah': Abraham's leap beyond the ethical into the religious models a resignation in which broken Hallelujahs are still worth singing, and The Sickness unto Death shows despair overcome by letting go of the ego so that suffering begets compassion and love.

Wieland Schwanebeck surveys the many masculinities in Cohen's songs - spies, soldiers, cowboys, rabbis, captains - and argues they mostly appear broken, mocked, or failing (the losing partisan, the captain whose ship leaks or crew deserts), which puts the 'real man' ideal in doubt. He shows how Cohen's Jewishness plays against stereotypes of the bookish, unathletic Jewish man, usually embraced and then inverted with Socratic irony, as in 'Is This What You Wanted' and 'Lover Lover Lover.' Following Judith Butler's Gender Trouble, he reads Cohen's stage persona - the tailored suit, kneeling, clowning, and erotic ambiguity - as a repeated performance demonstrating that masculinity is 'an imitation without an origin.'

Gary Shapiro treats The Future as a 'lyrical phenomenology' of time that stages multiple temporalities rather than one theory of time. 'The Future' evokes an apocalypse where the katechon - the Biblical restraining force holding back the end - no longer works, while 'Waiting for the Miracle' anatomizes passive deferral in a way Shapiro finds sharper than the Stoic critique of waiting by Seneca and Marcus Aurelius and Nietzsche's 'problem of those who wait,' opposing wasted chronos to the seized kairos of 'First We Take Manhattan.' 'Anthem's' crack that lets the light in gets a Gnostic reading, 'Democracy' is glossed through Derrida's 'democracy to come' as messianic, always-arriving futurity, and 'Closing Time' and 'Always' add honky-tonk eschatology and the vow of eternal love.

Jason Holt defends the serious question of whether Cohen is a good singer against both anti-fans and fandom, arguing that judgments of taste purport to objectivity and cannot be settled by polls or Juno Awards. Borrowing David Hume's standard of taste - ideal critics with strong sense, delicate sentiment, practice, comparison, and freedom from prejudice - he judges Cohen in his 'weight class' as a singer-songwriter and vocal stylist, ranks him between Paul Simon and Bob Dylan, and offers the 'great singer-songwriter argument' that excellence in both crafts implies being at least a good singer. Much dismissal, he argues, is really style prejudice or a category mistake, and he ends by confessing that Cohen's voice saved him from teenage suicide, biasing him in the best possible way.
